title: Provincial Benefit Finders
subtitle: You do not need to remember any of the last eight modules. You need to remember the tools that ask the questions for you.

blocks.text: You do not need to remember any of the last eight modules. That is not a joke at your expense, or ours.
You need to remember three or four tools that will ask you the questions instead.

A benefit finder is a short questionnaire. It asks your age, province, income range and household situation, plus a few checkboxes. Then it returns a list of programs you may qualify for, federal and provincial together. None of them replace this course. What they do is turn everything the last eight modules taught you into a fifteen-minute habit you can repeat every year, long after the details of Module 1.3 have faded.
A fifteen-minute check each year can catch programs you qualify for that nobody will ever mail you.
blocks.detail: Four free tools ask the questions for you, and each one finds things the others miss.
blocks.extra: Section 02 shows what each tool is good for.

sections.title: Four Tools, and What Each One Is Good For

blocks.text: Eight modules of programs, layers, lanes and money types is a lot to carry. Nobody is expected to hold it all in their head at tax time, during a renovation or the week after a layoff. What is worth carrying is much shorter.

items.title: The federal Benefits Finder
items.text: Run by the Government of Canada at canada.ca, this casts the widest net. Answer a short questionnaire, and it returns a list of federal, provincial and territorial programs for you. You do not need an account, and it does not track you after the session. It is a good place to start, because it does not assume you know which government is in charge of what.

items.title: Your provincial government’s own benefits page
items.text: Every province and territory has one. You can usually find it by searching your province’s name plus “benefits” or “find services.” British Columbia calls its version a Benefits Connector. These tend to be more current on provincial details than the federal tool, because the province updates its own programs.

Not a website first. A phone number. Dial 2-1-1 anywhere in Canada and reach a live person who knows local, provincial and some federal programs, including the ones that never make a government homepage: a municipal home repair program, a food bank’s income supports, a legal clinic’s hours.

items.title: The Benefits Wayfinder
items.text: Built by Prosper Canada, a national charity, not a government department. It is written in plain language for people with low and modest incomes, and you can use it alone or with a support worker. The federal tool casts the widest net. This one goes deepest for the people this course spends the most time on.

items.title: “These tools all show the same results, so it does not matter which one I use.”
items.text: They pull from similar, but not identical, sources. A provincial tool will often find a local program the federal one never mentions. The federal tool catches programs a provincial one has no reason to list. Running more than one is not a waste. It is how you would search for anything else you wanted to find completely.

blocks.text: Quick gut check: if the last time you ran one of these was more than a year ago, that is the whole lesson of this module, right there.

sections.title: The habit that matters more than any tool

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: RUN MORE THAN ONE, AND RUN THEM AGAIN NEXT YEAR

The most valuable habit in this module is not any one tool. It is doing the check every year, not just once. Who qualifies changes all the time, and quietly: a birthday that crosses an age limit, a change in household income, a new child, a diagnosis, a move to another province, or a program that launched last month. Someone who ran a benefit finder three years ago and found nothing is not wrong about three years ago. They may be wrong about now. Set a yearly reminder. Tax season works well, since your income numbers are already in front of you. Run the federal tool and your province’s tool every year, even when nothing feels different. The tools take fifteen minutes. Missing a program for three years because nobody checked again costs much more.

sections.title: What a benefit finder cannot do

blocks.text: It gives you a list, not an approval. Every result still means reading the real eligibility rules, gathering papers and applying through the real program, which is everything this course has spent nine modules teaching you to do well. Treat the finder as the map, not the destination.

It also cannot know what you do not tell it. If you round your income up, or skip a question about disability because it feels personal, the results match the version of your life you gave it, not your real life. These tools do not check anything. Their privacy notes say they usually do not keep your answers. That leaves little reason to hold back on a form that cannot be used against you later, and every reason to answer in full.

items.title: I have my rough household income and family situation ready before I start, so I am not guessing mid-questionnaire.
I am running both the federal tool and my province’s own tool, not just one.
I am answering every question completely, including ones that feel personal.
I am treating every result as a lead to verify, not a confirmed benefit.
I have a note of today’s date, since results reflect programs open right now.
I have set a reminder to do this again next year.

sections.title: Walter, a library computer, and the list he did not expect

paragraphs: Walter is seventy-three and lives alone outside Saskatoon. He has never in his life thought of himself as someone who applies for things. He worked and he paid his taxes. When his wife died three years ago, he assumed any help for that had already found him, the way his pension had.
His goal these days is simple: stay in the house he and his wife built, even as the stairs get harder.
One Saturday, his niece sits with him at the library to help him print a form. On a whim, she asks if he has ever run the federal Benefits Finder. He has not heard of it.

The questionnaire asks if he is a widower, and whether he has trouble getting around his home. Walter almost skips both. They feel private. Then he decides to answer every question honestly, since the form cannot be checked against him anyway.

Fifteen minutes later, the list shows two programs he knows and three he does not. One is a provincial home support program for seniors. Another is a survivor supplement nobody ever told him about. Nobody mails a letter announcing that a benefit exists. You have to go looking, or answer a questionnaire that looks for you.
On Monday, he calls 211 to check that the provincial program is real and still open. It is.
Walter applies within the week. By winter, someone comes twice a week to help around the house, and he is still in the home he and his wife built.

blocks.text: Run the federal Benefits Finder and your province’s own tool, not just one. Call 211 for anything local a web form would not know about. Answer every question in full, since the tools cannot check anything you do not tell them. Treat every result as a lead to check against the real program, and do it all again next year, because who qualifies changes quietly and often.
Walter found a home support program and a survivor supplement by answering every question, even the private ones.
blocks.detail: Fifteen honest minutes with a benefit finder can uncover help nobody will ever mail you.
blocks.extra: Your action this week, in Section 06, takes fifteen minutes.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Benefit-Finder Results

items.title: Run the federal Benefits Finder at canada.ca, answering every question completely.
Search your province’s name plus benefits finder, or call 211, and run the provincial equivalent.
Set a recurring yearly reminder, tied to tax season, to run both again, whether or not anything in your life feels like it has changed.

blocks.text: One rule of thumb: a program you did not recognize is not a mistake in the results. It is the entire reason to run the tool.

items.title: Benefits Finder
items.text: The federal government’s questionnaire at canada.ca. It shows federal, provincial and territorial results together.

items.title: Benefits Connector
items.text: British Columbia’s version of a provincial benefit-finder tool.

items.title: Benefits Wayfinder
items.text: A plain-language finder built by the charity Prosper Canada, for people with low and modest incomes.
A free phone line and, in many provinces, a website that connects you to local, provincial and some federal social and government services.

items.title: WHERE TO GET HELP
list: 211: dial 2-1-1 anywhere in Canada for a live person and the current local list.
Canada.ca Benefits Finder: the federal government’s own tool, no account required.
Your province’s own benefits page: search your province’s name plus benefits or find services.
Benefits Wayfinder: run through Prosper Canada, usable alone or with help from a community agency.

blocks.text: This module deliberately names tools rather than dollar amounts, since a finder’s job is to surface current programs. The figures live inside each result, not in the tool itself.
